learn.title: High availability for compute
objectives: Choose between availability sets, availability zones and Virtual Machine Scale Sets (Flexible orchestration) and know the VM SLA each one earns
Make App Service, Azure Functions, Azure Container Apps and AKS zone redundant, and know which settings must be chosen at creation time
Use zone-redundant Azure Load Balancer frontends, Application Gateway v2 and health probes as HA building blocks
Design multi-region active-active or active-passive compute with Azure Front Door, Traffic Manager or a global load balancer
Calculate composite SLAs and convert availability percentages into allowed downtime
concepts: Availability zone
A physically separate group of datacenters in a region with its own power, cooling and networking. Two or more VMs spread across two or more zones earn the 99.99% VM SLA.
Availability set
A logical grouping that spreads VMs across up to 3 fault domains and up to 20 update domains in one datacenter. Two or more VMs earn 99.95%. It does not protect against a datacenter or zone failure.
Fault domain vs update domain

A fault domain shares power and a network switch (like a rack). An update domain is a group of VMs that the platform restarts together during planned maintenance; only one update domain is restarted at a time.
Zonal vs zone-redundant

Zonal means pinned to one zone you choose (no zone resilience on its own). Zone-redundant (zone-spanning for scale sets) means instances spread across zones automatically. Nonzonal (regional) means Azure can place it anywhere, so any zone outage may affect it.
Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Flexible orchestration

The recommended mode. Manages standard VMs, up to 1,000 instances with fault domain guarantees, mixes VM sizes and Spot with on-demand, supports Azure Backup and attaching existing VMs. The orchestration mode can't be changed after creation.
Automatic instance repairs

A scale set feature that replaces (default), reimages or restarts instances reported unhealthy by the Application Health extension or a load balancer probe. Grace period 10-90 minutes (default 10); no more than 5% of instances repaired at once.
Proximity placement group
A colocation constraint that keeps VMs in the same datacenter for the lowest latency. It can't span zones, so it trades resiliency for latency.
Zone-redundant PaaS compute

App Service Premium v2-v4 (minimum 2 instances), Functions Flex Consumption, Premium or Dedicated (host storage must be ZRS), and Container Apps (set at environment creation, needs a virtual network). No extra charge for the feature itself, but minimum instance counts can raise cost.
AKS availability zones

The control plane is zone resilient by default in AZ regions. Node pool zones can't be added to an existing cluster. Standard or Premium tier gives 99.95% API server SLA with zones and 99.9% without; Free tier has no financially backed SLA.
Health probe

A periodic check that removes failed instances from rotation. Load Balancer probes come from 168.63.129.16 (AzureLoadBalancer service tag); HTTP probes need a 200. App Service Health check pings every minute and replaces an instance that stays unhealthy for one hour.
Composite SLA
For components in series, multiply their availabilities (for example 99.99% x 99.95% = about 99.94%). For redundant copies in parallel, availability = 1 - (product of each copy's unavailability).
Allowed downtime
Per month: 99.9% is about 43.2 minutes, 99.95% about 21.6 minutes, 99.99% about 4.32 minutes.
comparisons: Sets protect against rack and maintenance failures inside one datacenter (99.95%) and give lower VM-to-VM latency. Zones protect against loss of a whole datacenter (99.99%). Use sets only where zones aren't available or latency rules them out.
Flexible: standard VMs, mixed sizes and Spot, Azure Backup, attach VMs, Application Health extension for health. Uniform: identical instances, used by AKS and Service Fabric, no Azure Backup.
Front Door vs Traffic Manager vs global load balancer

Front Door: global HTTP(S) layer 7 entry point with fast failover and WAF. Traffic Manager: DNS-based, any protocol, failover delayed by DNS TTL and client caching. Global (cross-region) Load Balancer: layer 4 static anycast IP across regional public load balancers.
Zone redundancy set at creation vs changeable later

Fixed at creation: Container Apps environment, AKS cluster zones, Functions Premium plan, scale set orchestration mode, availability set fault/update domain counts. Changeable later: App Service plan (if the scale unit supports it), adding zones to a scale set, Load Balancer frontend (by adding a new frontend IP).

Active-active serves traffic from all regions and suits stateless HTTP workloads behind Front Door. Active-passive keeps a standby region idle, which suits event-driven processing where only one region should consume messages.
traps: A zone-redundant load balancer does not make the app zone resilient if every backend VM sits in one zone.
A zonal VM can't be moved to another zone; you deploy a new VM in the target zone.
Functions Consumption plan has no availability zone support; zone-redundant Premium and Flex Consumption need a ZRS host storage account.
Traffic Manager failover is not instant: clients keep using cached DNS answers until the TTL expires, and existing connections are not moved.
The AKS uptime SLA covers the Kubernetes API server, not your pods; you still need multiple replicas, zonal node pools and PodDisruptionBudgets.
Composite SLA in series is always lower than the weakest component; adding a global entry point can cap a multi-region design.
revision: Two or more VMs across two or more zones = 99.99%; availability set or fault-domain-spread flexible scale set = 99.95%; single VM with Premium SSD = 99.9%.
Flexible scale sets are the recommended VM HA option; zone-spanning gives the highest SLA.
App Service zone redundancy: Premium v2-v4, at least two instances; over-provision because replacement capacity in a zone outage is best effort.
Container Apps zone redundancy is chosen when the environment is created, needs a virtual network and at least two replicas.
Application Gateway v2 is zone-redundant by default in the portal and needs zone redundancy or autoscale to qualify for its SLA.
Health endpoints should test critical dependencies and return 200 only when the instance can really serve traffic.
Use Front Door for global HTTP active-active, Traffic Manager for DNS-based routing of any protocol, and a global load balancer for layer 4 anycast.
